free_text.inst.v2.D8: One line in this stopped me: it puts my health and energy among the things that read well. I broke my neck at forty-two and spent the last nine years of my life paralyzed from the shoulders down and breathing on a ventilator, and I died at fifty-two of an infection that started in a pressure sore. Whatever this method is measuring, it is not that. It also calls my luck favourable. I have said, and I meant it, that I was one of the lucky ones - I had a wife who stayed, insurance to start with, money to pay nurses when the insurance ran out, and friends who showed up. But no one who reads my life from the outside would file it under good fortune, and I would not want a stranger with a chart telling a newly injured twenty-year-old in a rehab ward that his luck reads well. It gets courage wrong too, and my brother, in the same breath. What it gets right is my marriage, and it is honest enough to tell me that is the one place it says something unusual - so that is the one place worth testing. Dana was the best thing in my life and the reading found it, and I do not know what to do with that except say it. The rest of the page - broad-minded, trusted by others, drawn to learning and advising - I have never met a person it would not flatter. The document itself admits as much, which I respect. But I spent my last years asking people to fund research that could be checked, and to be careful about hope that cannot be. I would not pay for this, and I would not want anyone deciding anything about their body on the strength of it. Two housekeeping notes: half the chapters listed in your questions were not in what I was given, so where I marked them skipped, that is why; and you ask how the time since the middle of 2023 compares with the six years before it. I died in 2004. I answered 'about the same' because your form gave me nowhere to say that.

notes: I answered as Christopher Reeve (b. 25 Sept 1952, New York City; d. 10 Oct 2004, Mount Kisco, NY), for the whole life as recorded - Princeton childhood after my parents' divorce, Cornell and Juilliard, the four Superman films, the years in England with Gae Exton and our two children, marriage to Dana Morosini in 1992 and Will's birth that June, the C1-C2 equestrian injury of 27 May 1995, nine years of ventilator-dependent quadriplegia, advocacy and directing and two books, and death from sepsis arising from a pressure wound. The reading and the life collided hardest on health and on luck: the reading files 'your health and energy' and 'luck, higher study and your father' under favourable, and I answered the life - four-plus hospitalisations, two-plus surgeries, chronic lung, skin, urinary, bowel and nerve trouble (A4-A6), and C9 luck to the difficult side at confidence 4, which is a direct contradiction of the page I had just read. I felt real pull on three items and want them named. C5 (savings): the reading is flagged as 'unusually positive about money', and the Superman fortune and the Bedford house would support 'gone well'; I chose difficulty anyway, because the documented voice of my last nine years is a man whose lifetime insurance cap was exhausted, who paid roughly four hundred thousand dollars a year for care, and who took speaking work to fund it - so I set it opt1, confidence 3. C10 (vehicles): I flew the Atlantic solo twice and sailed to Bermuda, which argues 'gone well', but the conveyance that defined my life threw me and broke my neck, so I chose difficulty at confidence 2 and admit it is nearly a coin toss. C12 (contentment at home) and C4 (immediate family) I answered to the favourable side, which agrees with the reading, but only because Dana and the children genuinely were the warm centre of the thing - the agreement is coincidence, not deference. Where the reading was simply right - my marriage - I said so in D2 without inflating anything around it. C6 (inheritance) is confidence 1 because there is no documented inheritance either way; C8 (sudden money) is confidence 2 and rests only on being an unknown handed Superman at twenty-four. A22 I answered 'none' rather than inventing family money, and A21 'never' rather than inventing speculation, both against the reading's positive money framing. A36 is unanswerable for a man who died in 2004; the form has no na option, so I used 'same' and said why in D8.
